q: Go was created at which company, and first released in which year?
explain: Designed at Google by Griesemer, Pike and Thompson; open-sourced in 2009. Boredom with C++ build times was a founding motive.

q: Which of these is NOT a Go keyword?
explain: Go has 25 keywords and lambda is not one — anonymous functions are just func literals: func() { … }.

q: What does GOMAXPROCS control?
a: Max OS threads running user code at once
explain: It caps OS threads executing Go code (default: CPU count). Goroutines multiplex on top — tons of goroutines, few threads.
options: Max OS threads running user code at once

q: Which symbol starts an exported (public) identifier?
explain: Capitalization IS the access modifier: Foo is public, foo is package-private. No public/private keywords exist.

q: What does gofmt enforce?
a: One canonical format for all Go code
explain: gofmt ends style debates — tabs, brace placement, alignment are fixed. Run gofmt -l in CI to catch drift.
options: One canonical format for all Go code

q: A nil slice and an empty slice differ in what way?
a: Only in == nil comparison and JSON null vs []
explain: Both have len 0 and both append fine. They differ only for == nil checks and JSON encoding (null vs []).
options: Only in == nil comparison and JSON null vs []

q: True or false: Go supports method overloading.
a: False — one name, one signature per type
explain: No overloading in Go. Variants get distinct names (Parse, ParseBytes, MustParse) — which arguably reads better.
options: False — one name, one signature per type

q: What is a goroutine, roughly?
explain: Goroutines start around 2KB and grow as needed, scheduled by the Go runtime onto OS threads. Concurrency without thread-pool plumbing.

q: Which verb prints a value with Go-syntax formatting?
explain: %#v prints the Go-syntax form (great for debugging structs), %T prints the type, %d is decimal integers.

q: How many return values can a Go function have?
explain: Go functions return any number of values — the (value, error) pair is just convention, not a limit.

q: Which tool fixes imports and formats in one pass?
explain: goimports is gofmt plus automatic import management: adds missing imports, drops unused ones. Most editors run it on save.

q: What happens if main() returns while goroutines still run?
explain: main returning ends the process — no joining, no cleanup. That is why examples pair go f() with WaitGroups or channels.

q: Which of these types is comparable with ==?
explain: Slices, maps and funcs are only comparable to nil. Arrays compare fine — one of several reasons slices won and arrays faded.

q: What does defer do with its function call?
a: Schedules it to run when the surrounding func returns
explain: Deferred calls run LIFO at return — perfect for Unlock, Close, and cleanup that must happen on every path.
options: Schedules it to run when the surrounding func returns

q: How do you check your Go version?
explain: go version prints the toolchain. go env shows the full configuration (GOPATH, GOFLAGS, module cache…).

q: What is the zero value of a pointer, slice, map, channel and func?
explain: Reference-ish types all start nil. Reading through most nils is safe-ish; writing through them is not.

q: Who designed Go?
a: Pike, Thompson and Griesemer at Google
explain: Rob Pike and Ken Thompson (Unix and UTF-8 legends) plus Robert Griesemer. Serious pedigree, zero interest in language fashion.
options: Pike, Thompson and Griesemer at Google

q: What did GOPATH hold before modules took over?
a: All third-party source, binaries and builds
explain: Pre-modules, every dependency lived in one global GOPATH workspace. Version conflicts were a lifestyle. Modules ended the dark age.
options: All third-party source, binaries and builds

q: Which keyword launches a goroutine?
explain: Two letters. The cheapest concurrency keyword in any mainstream language, and the runtime does the hard parts.

q: What is the zero value of the error type?
explain: A nil error means success — the entire if-err-nil idiom rests on this. A non-nil error with empty text is still an error.

q: What is Delve?
explain: Delve is the debugger: breakpoints, stepping, goroutine inspection. dlv debug beats Println archaeology.

q: What is gopls?
a: The Go language server for editors
explain: gopls powers autocomplete, go-to-definition and renames in VS Code, Vim, Emacs and friends. One daemon, every editor.
options: The Go language server for editors

q: Go binaries are static by default. What does that buy you?
a: Single-file deploys with no runtime to install
explain: One binary that runs anywhere: scratch containers, tiny VMs, your Raspberry Pi. Deployment becomes copying a file.
options: Single-file deploys with no runtime to install

q: Which two env vars cross-compile for Windows on ARM?
explain: Set GOOS and GOARCH and go build emits a foreign binary with zero toolchain fuss. Demo it at parties.

q: What does the race detector cost, roughly?
a: 2-10x slower builds — worth it in CI anyway
explain: Instrumentation is not free, but neither are 3am data-race pages. Race in CI, full speed locally.
options: 2-10x slower builds — worth it in CI anyway

q: What is errgroup (golang.org/x/sync)?
a: WaitGroup that collects the first error
explain: errgroup fans out goroutines like WaitGroup, but Wait returns the first non-nil error. Concurrency with accountability.
options: WaitGroup that collects the first error

q: Which two files pin every dependency version?
explain: go.mod declares requirements, go.sum holds the hashes. Commit both or dependency roulette begins.

q: How do you update all dependencies to latest minor versions?
explain: The -u flag bumps to newest minor and patch versions. Majors need explicit paths since v2+ changes import paths. Read the diff before pushing.

q: What does GOROOT point at?
explain: GOROOT is where Go itself lives. You almost never set it by hand anymore — the toolchain found its own home.

q: Does go test run vet checks too?
explain: go test quietly runs key vet checks (printf verbs, struct tags) before your tests. Redundant safety net, zero config.

q: What does a dot import do?
a: Merges the package into your namespace
explain: import . "pkg" drops the qualifier: Fmt.Println becomes Println. Convenient in tests, a readability hazard everywhere else.
options: Merges the package into your namespace

q: type A = B versus type A B?
explain: The equals sign is the whole difference: alias shares identity (and methods), definition starts fresh. Refactors hinge on one character.

q: What is 1 << iota famous for?
a: Bit-flag enums that double each line
explain: Shifted iota mints powers of two: Read=1, Write=2, Exec=4. OR them together, AND to test. Flag sets without a library.
options: Bit-flag enums that double each line

q: Can a package have multiple init() funcs?
a: Yes — even several per file, run in order
explain: Go runs every init in dependency order, file by file, top to bottom. Powerful, implicit, and exactly why veterans keep init tiny.
options: Yes — even several per file, run in order

q: Which package does regex?
explain: regexp with MustCompile for baked-in patterns, Compile for user input. RE2 syntax: all the power, none of the catastrophic backtracking.

q: What does go env GOPATH show now?
a: Module cache home and legacy workspace root
explain: Post-modules, GOPATH mostly hosts the download cache and build artifacts. Your code can live anywhere — freedom previous generations dreamed of.
options: Module cache home and legacy workspace root

q: What happens on an unused import?
explain: Go treats unused imports as errors, not warnings. Annoying for exactly three days, then your editor auto-manages them and you never look back.

q: Methods on another package's types?
explain: Go forbids adding methods to types you do not own. Wrap the foreign type in your own named type and extend that instead.

q: Why is Go map iteration order deliberately random?
a: To stop you depending on any order
explain: The runtime shuffles it on purpose: code that assumes an order breaks fast in testing instead of silently in production.
options: To stop you depending on any order
It isn't — maps sort by key

q: What does len() of a nil slice return?
explain: nil slices behave like empty ones for len, cap, range and append. Only indexing or writing panics.

q: Binary search on a million sorted ints takes about how many steps?
explain: 2^20 is roughly a million. Halving wins so hard it feels like cheating — that is O(log n).

q: Indexing past the end of a slice does what?
explain: Go bounds-checks every access and panics instead of handing you garbage. The <= in for i <= len(s) is the classic trigger.

q: Appending to a full slice does what behind the curtain?
explain: No room means a new bigger backing array plus a full copy. That copy is why append returns a header you must keep — and why batch appends beat one-by-one growth.
options: Extends the same array in place

q: Floyd's tortoise and hare detects what?
explain: Fast gains one node per round on a loop, so it must land on slow. Meeting without hitting nil proves a cycle; hitting nil proves a clean list.
